newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gives boost to moderate Chechen leader.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gives boost to moderate Chechen leader.

text.p: A deal signed by President Boris Yeltsin and Aslan Maskhadov may outrage Russia's hawks, but is certain to help the relatively moderate Chechen leader keep his devastated region under control and the peace process on track.

Maskhadov, who led Chechnya's forces in their 21-month war against Russian forces sent there to crush the independence bid, was welcomed as an equal by the Russian president in the Grand Kremlin Palace.

"I want to welcome the president of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria," Yeltsin told Maskhadov as the two men met, using the Chechen's own name for their self-proclaimed region -- until now something of a taboo word in Moscow.
The two signed a peace deal and proclaimed a new era in the bitter history of relations between the two nations.
"Today we have ended the 400-year confrontation, regardless of those who wanted the war to continue," said Maskhkadov.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Russian government envoy in Chechnya, Georgy Kurin, as saying the peace deal did not touch upon the region's future status, something which is due not to be discussed until 2003 under a peace deal agreed last year.
The meeting was in stark contrast to one last year between Yeltsin and former Chechen leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who was treated curtly as an unruly regional boss.
Maskhadov, who won Chechnya's presidential election in January, was clearly delighted at his own reception.
"Now we will prove to the whole world that the Chechen authorities and its president are in control," he told Yeltsin after signing the peace accord.
"There will be no more place in Chechnya for terrorists and kidnappers," he added, giving Yeltsin an argument to defend the deal at home.

Maskhadov, wearing his trademark tall fur hat, now faces the double task of feeding the population of the devastated region and staying in tune with the pro-independence mood among influential field commanders.
If he makes too many concessions to Moscow he may face a mutiny from his former comrades-in-arms. If he allows Moscow to blockade Chechnya he could be swept away by public anger.

Maskhadov's welcome in Moscow and a series of economic agreements with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin clearly improved his chances of consolidating power in Chechnya without making dramatic concessions.

Yeltsin has also faced problems both from hawks, who wanted him to delay the meeting with Maskhadov, and doves, who said the moderate leader could be replaced by a hardliner unless the meeting took place.
By calling the meeting now, the Kremlin leader has finally made his choice.

The hawks, led by Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, say rebel leaders will never agree to keep the region as part of Russia and say their inability to control armed fighters is to blame for a series of kidnappings and blasts in southern Russia.
They insist the Chechen leaders be treated harshly and say Chechnya should not get any financial help until it surrenders to Kremlin demands.

The doves, led by Yeltsin's close aides Ivan Rybkin and Boris Berezovsky, say economic factors may keep Chechnya firmly inside Russia and insist the Chechen leaders should not be pushed into a corner if the sides are to find a mutually acceptable formula for coexistance.

"Some parts of the document seem appropriate for inter-state relations rather than for relation between the federal centre and one of the regions," RIA news agency quoted parliamentary deputy Vladimir Lysenko as saying.
"This may prompt a scandal in the State Duma lower house," he added indicating possible complications.
But Yeltsin appeared unconcerned.
"It does not matter how many articles this document have. A peace deal has been signed and that's what it all means," he told reporters after signing."
